Pilot training

Europe or the USA? Compare the routes.

Where you train decides which rules apply and which licence you get. Start from where you want to work, then compare.

Side by side

EASA and FAA at a glance.

A plain-language comparison to help you prepare questions. It does not replace advice from the training organisation or the authority.

Comparison of European EASA and US FAA pilot training
Europe · EASAUSA · FAA
Who sets the rulesThe European Union Aviation Safety Agency sets the framework. A national authority issues your licence.The US Federal Aviation Administration sets the rules and issues certificates.
What you holdLicences such as PPL, CPL and ATPL, plus ratings such as the instrument rating (IR).Certificates such as private pilot, commercial pilot and ATP, plus ratings such as the instrument rating.
How training is structuredIntegrated (one structured programme) or modular (in stages).Usually in stages, often under Part 61 or Part 141 school rules.
Likely cost componentsTuition, flight and simulator hours, exams and fees, medical, accommodation, living costs, equipment, contingency.Tuition or hourly rates, exams and checkrides, medical, visa, accommodation, living costs, contingency.
Questions to checkWhich authority issues the licence? What does an integrated course include? What if training takes longer?How would certificates convert where I want to work? What does the visa allow? What is included in the hourly rate?

Guidance prepared November 2026 for the EU (EASA) and US (FAA) jurisdictions. Rules change, so always confirm with the authority and the school.

Integrated or modular

Two ways to structure training.

Compare outcome, pace, what is included and the career market you are aiming for. Neither is right for everyone.

01

Integrated

One structured programme, usually full-time, from little or no experience towards commercial and instrument qualifications. Finishing it doesn’t by itself award a full ATPL.

02

Modular

Training in separate stages, sometimes with schools or breaks in between. It can be more flexible, but you need to plan the whole sequence yourself.

Check for your situation

Questions to verify before you choose.

These depend on you and must be confirmed with the right source.

  • Medical certificate requirements, with an approved aviation medical examiner.
  • Visa and residence rules, with the relevant embassy or authority.
  • Licence conversion for the country where you want to work, with that country’s authority.
  • Employment prospects. Airlines make their own hiring decisions.

Glossary

Terms in plain English.

Tap a term to see what it means.

EASA

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency. It sets the common framework for pilot licensing in Europe.

FAA

The Federal Aviation Administration, the aviation authority of the United States.

Licence / certificate

Describes what a pilot is allowed to do. Europe says “licence”, the USA says “certificate”.

Rating

An extra qualification added to a licence, such as an instrument rating.

PPL

Private pilot licence. Lets you fly privately, not for pay.

CPL

Commercial pilot licence. Lets you be paid to fly in some roles.

IR

Instrument rating. Lets you fly using instruments in poor visibility.

ATPL / ATP

Airline transport pilot licence (Europe) or certificate (USA), the highest level. It requires exams and significant flight experience.

“Frozen ATPL”

Informal shorthand, not an official licence. Ask exactly which licence, exams and ratings someone means.

Integrated / modular

Integrated is one structured programme. Modular is training in separate stages.
